title: How Much a Personal Injury Lawyer Costs: Fees Explained
description: Most personal injury lawyers use contingency fees, but clients still need a clear breakdown of percentages, expenses, and what happens if the case does not recover money.
meta_description: Most personal injury lawyers charge a contingency fee of about one third of the recovery, more at trial, plus case expenses. How fees work and what to ask.
main_html:
Personal Injury Lawyer Fees Explained: what should you know?

Educational only. Not legal advice. No endorsements or rankings.

Most personal injury lawyers work on a contingency fee, which means the fee usually comes out of any recovery rather than being billed up front.

“No win, no fee” is only a headline. The real comparison is the percentage before filing, the percentage after filing, what case costs are separate, whether expenses are deducted before or after the fee, and how liens affect the final payout.

How Much Does a Personal Injury Lawyer Cost?

  • Typical pre-suit range: many agreements use a lower percentage before litigation starts.
  • Typical litigation range: the percentage may increase if a lawsuit is filed or the case moves deeper into litigation.
  • Costs and expenses: case costs are often tracked separately from the lawyer's fee.
  • If you lose: what you owe depends on the written agreement and how costs are handled.

Worked example

If a case settles for $100,000, the fee percentage applies to the recovery and expenses may also be deducted depending on the agreement. The only safe way to know the net amount is to ask for a written example using your firm's actual fee language.

What a contingency fee actually means: what should you know?

A contingency fee is a payment arrangement where the lawyer's fee is tied to recovery. It is still important to read how costs, liens, and timing are handled in the contract.

“No win, no fee” is only a headline. The real comparison is the percentage before filing, the percentage after filing, what case costs are separate, whether expenses are deducted before or after the fee, and how liens affect the final payout.

When to ask fee questions early: what should you know?

Ask fee questions early, before you feel urgency to sign. If the numbers or timing are unclear in the first consultation, be careful and slow down.

How Do Contingency Fees Work?

  1. You sign a written fee agreement.
  2. The firm opens the case and tracks work and expenses.
  3. The case resolves through settlement or litigation.
  4. Fees and costs are deducted according to the agreement.
  5. The client receives the net amount that remains.

What documents help you verify fees: what should you know?

Ask for the written agreement, sample settlement math, and documentation showing how records, expenses, and reimbursements are handled.

Questions worth asking about fees: what should you know?

  • What percentage applies before a lawsuit is filed?
  • What changes if the case goes into litigation?
  • Which costs are separate from the fee?
  • What happens if there is no recovery?

Fee red flags: what should you know?

Red flags include vague answers, pressure to sign before the math is clear, or resistance when you ask for a written example.

What to do next: what should you know?

Use the consultation questions guide so every firm explains fees the same way before you compare your options.

Contingency fees, hidden costs, and questions to ask before signing: what should you know?

Many personal injury lawyers use contingency fees, which means the lawyer is paid from a recovery instead of charging hourly upfront. The important details are the percentage, whether the percentage changes if litigation starts, who advances case costs, and what happens if there is no recovery.

  • Ask for the contingency percentage in writing.
  • Ask whether case expenses are deducted before or after the fee is calculated.
  • Ask what costs you could owe if the case does not recover money.
  • Ask how medical liens, health insurance claims, and settlement checks are handled.

Quick FAQ

Is “no win, no fee” always literal? Not always. It may describe attorney fees but not every case expense, lien, or medical balance.

What fee range should I expect? Many contingency agreements are percentage-based; the exact percentage and cost treatment must be reviewed in the written agreement.

Fee data and agreement review checklist: what should you know?

Do not rely on “no fee unless we win” as the full fee explanation. Ask for the written agreement and compare these fields before signing.

Fee fieldWhat to verify
Contingency percentageWhether it changes after filing, litigation, or trial preparation.
Case expensesWho advances costs and whether costs are deducted before or after attorney fees.
Medical liensHow bills, liens, reimbursements, and settlement deductions are handled.
No recoveryWhat happens to expenses if the case does not recover money.

Contingency Fee Review Checklist: what should you know?

Compare written fee terms instead of relying on no-win-no-fee slogans.

  • Fee percentage before and after filing
  • Case costs and when they are deducted
  • Medical liens and reimbursements
  • What happens if there is no recovery
  • Request a written net-recovery example

Educational only. No rankings, endorsements, medical advice, legal advice, or outcome promises.

What is the answer?

A settlement figure is a gross number. What reaches you is that number minus the fee, minus case expenses, minus any liens.

There are really two cost questions, and they have different answers. The first is what comes off the top when the case succeeds. The second is what the case costs you if it does not. A fee agreement answers both, and it is the only document that does.

Ask for a worked disbursement example before you sign a fee agreement. Every one of these deductions is knowable in advance.

Timing: what should you know?

The fee agreement is signed at the start, and it governs everything afterwards. That is the moment to ask these questions, not later.

Statutory deadlines to file vary by state and are often shorter than people expect. If you are near one, treat it as urgent.

Early is also when medical documentation is easiest to gather, which is the other reason not to wait.

The order the money comes off: what should you know?

DeductionWhat it isWhat to establish in writing first
Contingency feeA percentage of the gross recoveryThe percentage, and whether it rises if the case is filed or tried
Case expensesFiling fees, records, experts, depositions, imagingWhether expenses come off before or after the fee is calculated
Medical liensProviders or insurers claiming repayment from the settlementWhich liens exist, and who negotiates them down
Outstanding balancesUnpaid bills owed directly to providersWhat remains unpaid and at what amount
Net to youWhat is leftA worked example at a realistic settlement figure

Whether expenses are deducted before or after the fee changes the arithmetic materially. Get that answer in writing.

Two further details change the same arithmetic and are easy to miss. A tiered fee that rises once a case is filed, or once it is set for trial, is common; what matters is knowing which event triggers the step and who decides whether it happens. And where a case is handled by more than one firm, the fee is normally divided between them rather than added together, so the question to ask is whether any referral or co-counsel arrangement changes your total at all. If the answer is not a flat no, ask for it in writing.

What it costs if the case does not succeed: what should you know?

A contingency fee is contingent by definition: no recovery, no fee. Case expenses are a separate question, and the answer is not standard across firms.

Some agreements have the firm advance expenses and absorb them if the case fails. Others have the firm advance them and leave the client owing them regardless of outcome. Both are real arrangements, and the difference does not show up in the fee percentage at all — which is why comparing two firms on percentage alone can be misleading. Ask the question directly: if we recover nothing, what do I owe, and to whom.

There is a second exposure worth asking about. In some courts a losing party can be ordered to pay certain of the other side's costs, which is a narrower category than their legal fees but is not nothing. Whether that applies, and to what, depends on the court and the kind of case. It belongs on the list of things to establish before filing, not after.

Liens: the deduction that surprises people: what should you know?

Liens and repayment claims are the part of the disbursement that most often turns out larger than expected, and also the part that most often moves. Several different things sit in this category.

  • A health insurer that paid for treatment may claim repayment out of the settlement.
  • Government health programmes generally have statutory recovery rights, and those usually have to be identified and resolved before money can be released.
  • Many states allow hospitals to assert a lien against an injury recovery.
  • A provider who agreed to treat and wait for payment may hold a letter of protection, which functions much like a lien at disbursement.

Two practical points follow. First, these amounts are frequently negotiable, and a reduction goes straight to the client, so who does that negotiating and whether it is included in the fee is a fair question to ask at the start. Second, resolving a government repayment claim can take time after a settlement is agreed, which means a lien is a timing cost as well as a money cost. Ask what the realistic gap is between agreeing a number and receiving one.

A cost that is actually published: what should you know?

Most case expenses are not published anywhere. Court filing fees are.

In federal district court, the administrative fee is "$55" for filing a civil action, alongside the $350 statutory fee set by 28 U.S.C. § 1914(a) — $405 in total (District Court Miscellaneous Fee Schedule, effective 1 December 2023).

Most personal injury cases are filed in state court, where fees are set locally and vary. Ask your attorney for the figure in your county.

It is worth keeping the filing fee in proportion. It is the one expense with a published price, and usually among the smallest. The expenses that actually determine whether a case is worth investigating are the ones with no list price: retained experts, depositions and the transcripts of them, obtaining and reviewing medical records and imaging, and any reconstruction work. Those are the numbers to ask about, and the reason a firm may decline a case whose liability picture is sound but whose likely recovery would not cover proving it.

Questions to ask before signing: what should you know?

  • What is the fee percentage, and does it change at any stage?
  • Are expenses deducted before or after the fee?
  • Who advances expenses, and what happens if we lose?
  • If we recover nothing, what do I owe, and to whom?
  • Which liens do you expect, and who negotiates them?
  • Is lien negotiation covered by the fee or billed separately?
  • Does any referral or co-counsel arrangement change my total?
  • How long after a settlement is agreed should I expect to be paid?
  • Can I see a worked disbursement on a settlement of this size?

Common mistake: asking about the percentage and nothing else.

Tax treatment, and what not to assume: what should you know?

The IRS publishes this directly. For personal physical injuries or physical sickness, where you did not previously take an itemised deduction for related medical expenses, "the full amount is non-taxable" (Publication 4345, rev. 9-2023).

But if you did deduct those medical expenses in a prior year, you must include that portion in income to the extent the deduction gave you a tax benefit.

Do not assume the whole settlement is tax-free, and be careful with any allocation you have not read. Slow down before signing a release that allocates the settlement between categories.

The same caution applies to how a settlement is described in the release. An allocation between categories of damages can carry tax consequences, and it is written by someone other than you. Read it, and ask what each line is for before signing rather than afterwards.

What to do next: what should you know?

Ask for the worked disbursement example in writing. If the answer is vague at the start, it will not get clearer at the end.

A reasonable test of a fee conversation is whether you leave it able to state three things without looking them up: the fee and what moves it, who carries the expenses if the case fails, and which repayment claims are expected to come out of any recovery. If any of the three is still unclear, that is the question to go back with.

search_strengthening.query: how much does a personal injury lawyer cost
search_strengthening.definition: Most personal injury lawyers charge a contingency fee: no upfront payment, and a percentage of whatever you recover, commonly about one third, often rising to around 40 percent if the case goes to trial. Case expenses such as filing fees, records and expert witnesses are separate, and the agreement should say who pays them if you lose.

faq.q: What are average personal injury attorney fees?
faq.a: A contingency fee of about 33 percent of the recovery is the most common, with many agreements stepping up to 35 to 40 percent if a lawsuit is filed or the case goes to trial. Some states cap fees in certain cases, such as medical malpractice.

faq.q: How are expenses handled in personal injury legal fees?
faq.a: Expenses are separate from the fee. Ask whether they come out of the settlement before or after the percentage is calculated, because that changes what you take home, and whether you owe them if the case is lost.

faq.q: How much does a personal injury lawyer charge for a consultation?
faq.a: Usually nothing. Most personal injury firms offer a free first consultation and charge no fee unless they recover money for you.

faq.q: Can I negotiate a personal injury lawyer's fee?
faq.a: Often, yes, especially for a clear-liability case likely to settle quickly. Get the percentage, any step-ups and the expense terms in a signed written agreement before work starts.
